title: staggered-canary-feedback-loop-memory-pressure-and-rollout-abort-notes
content:
Summary:

On 2025-11-04 at ~04:30 UTC we observed a progressive p95/p99 latency increase in the hosted inference fleet in us-west-2 that correlated with a canary rollout of model variant v3.1-opt. The rollout used a staggered + traffic-shift policy (10% -> 25% -> 50%) over 90 minutes. Around the 25% step the canary pool experienced increasing OOM / memory pressure events and high KV-cache evictions which led to timeouts upstream and a cascade of retries. Because of a routing config mismatch one edge region (us-west-2b) received ~45% of the canary traffic during the 25% step, amplifying the load and triggering an automated rollout abort at 05:12 UTC.

Why this is unique / notes to self:
- Not a simple bad-weight file or checksum issue; two subtler pieces combined: a KV-cache retention mismatch in the v3.1-opt runtime build and an accidental skew in traffic routing weights for a subset of edge routers.
- The incident was triggered only under a specific prompt distribution pattern — a set of long conversational contexts from a small set of customers that produced large KV entries and prevented expected cache compaction heuristics from keeping memory under target.

Timeline (concise):
- 04:28 UTC: Canary rollout started (10% -> 25% step scheduled).
- 04:45 UTC: Automated telemetry alert: p95 token latency up 2.4x for model v3.1-opt (us-west-2b).
- 04:50 UTC: SRE on-call (Aisha) spotted elevated mem.usage on canary nodes and increased kv-cache eviction rate in console.
- 05:00 UTC: Upstream request timeouts increased, client SDKs retrying.
- 05:05 UTC: Traffic inspection via router metrics showed one subset of edge routers reporting 44–48% of canary traffic.
- 05:12 UTC: Rollout controller issued abort & traffic rebalanced to stable variant; rollout abort recorded in progress log.
- 05:20 UTC: Manual scale-up + temporary bump in cache memory limit applied to canary nodes to stabilize.
- 05:40 UTC: Latency returned to baseline; automated alerts cleared by 06:05 UTC.

Detection and signals:
- Primary: p95/p99 token latency + request timeout rate spiking for only the canary model ID.
- Secondary: node RSS and container OOM events followed by high KV eviction rates reported by runtime metrics (kv_eviction.count, kv_cache.size_bytes).
- Tertiary: router traffic distribution metrics (router.alloc_percent_by_pool) that highlighted skewed distribution.

Immediate mitigations performed (what worked):
- Abort rollout via controller (fast rollback to stable variant) — prevented further exposure.
- Rebalanced traffic at routing layer to fix skewed edge weights (quick fix: revert last edge-router config push).
- Increased canary pod memory limit by +25% as a temporary stopgap so the still-running canary pods could finish inflight requests without OOMing.
- Added transient token-rate-limiter on the affected tenant prefix to reduce super-long-context requests while we stabilized.

What didn't help / caused noise:
- Horizontal autoscaling on canary pool was too slow because autoscaler trigger threshold uses 5-min window for memory; memory rise was rapid and local.
- A previous patch to the runtime (PR #4182) changed kv-entry ttl semantics for long-session caching — intended optimization — which in practice kept entries alive longer and prevented eviction heuristics from reclaiming memory quickly. That patch alone was fine at 10% traffic but failed under skewed concentrated load.

Root cause analysis (hypothesis -> evidence):
- Hypothesis A: The kv-cache retention TTL change in v3.1-opt increased per-session KV size and delayed eviction. Evidence: runtime metrics show average kv_entry_size up 3.7x for canary and kv_entry_ttl median increased from 4m -> 37m for that build.
- Hypothesis B: Traffic routing misconfiguration directed disproportionately more canary traffic to a subset of routers that are CPU/memory constrained. Evidence: router.alloc_percent_by_pool logs for the rollout window show 44–48% concentrated allocation (should be ~25%).
- Hypothesis C: Combined effect produced local memory pressure -> eviction thrash -> increased page faults -> latency and timeouts. Evidence: node-level vmstat shows increased pgfaults and dstat shows swap usage spikes aligned with latency spikes.

Contributing factors:
- Rollout policy used narrow time windows and assumed uniform traffic distribution across edge routers; this assumption is fragile.
- Autoscaling policy thresholds (5m memory window) and step-down/up cooldowns made rapid response ineffective.
- Insufficient pre-rollout synthetic load for long-context prompts; our canary test corpus didn't include heavy tail session lengths.

Post-incident actions (short-term fixes done immediately):
- Reverted the kv-ttl change in runtime build for next quick canary (PR revert queued).
- Patched router control plane to prevent accidental skew on staggered rollouts; added validation that a single ASG/edge-subset cannot receive >1.5x intended weight without explicit override.
- Lowered autoscaler memory trigger window to 60s for canary pools (experimentally) and added a burst-scale path for memory pressure events.
- Added a temporary runtime metric alert: kv_entry_ttl_median > 10m and kv_cache.size_bytes growth > 30% in 2m should trigger canary pause.

Longer-term action items (owners and ETA):
- (Runtime) Rework kv cache compaction heuristics to be SLA-aware: ensure LRU fallback under memory pressure — Owner: Ravi Kumar; ETA: 2026-01-15.
- (Release) Add mandatory synthetic workload step for long-context prompts into canary gate CI — Owner: Evelyn Cho; ETA: 2025-12-10.
- (Routing) Implement rollout-weight sanity checks in rollout-controller (hard guardrails) — Owner: Miguel Santos; ETA: 2025-12-01.
- (SRE) Add a dedicated canary observability dashboard showing cross-metric blast radius (latency, kv_eviction, router_alloc) — Owner: Aisha Patel; ETA: 2025-11-18.
- (Runbook) Update staggered-rollout runbook to include immediate checks for router.alloc_percent_by_pool and kv_entry_ttl distribution; add explicit abort thresholds. Owner: SRE-runbooks team; ETA: 2025-11-12.

Monitoring & runbook changes (draft):
- Before advancing canary steps, validate:
  * router.alloc_percent_by_pool variance < 10% across ASGs for the target model id.
  * kv_cache.size_bytes growth < 20% in 3m under the canary.
  * synthetic long-context warmup pass completes within token-latency SLO.
- If any check fails, rollout should pause and notify on-call with the 'canary-pause' surge page.
- Add one-click rollback button in console that triggers both controller abort and router rebalancing to stable weights.

Unresolved questions / follow-ups:
- How did the router config drift happen? Need audit of last 48h router control plane changes (ticketed).
- KV TTL change rationale: was there limited canary telemetry before merge? Check PR notes + perf test logs.
- Confirm whether any customers saw model output regressions (the abort minimized impact, but customer telemetry needs cross-check).

Lessons learned (TL;DR):
- Small config changes (kv-ttl semantics) can be amplified by distribution skews. Canary policies must assume non-uniform traffic and validate distribution before stepping.
- Observability should surface resource pressure in higher-level rollout checks (not just node metrics).
- Autoscaling needs faster paths for memory spikes for in-flight canary traffic.

Appendices / artifacts:
- Quick links: Linear INC-7823 (postmortem tracking), PR #4182 (kv-ttl change), router-audit-20251104 (internal audit artifact).
- Raw logs: attached in linked artifact (Slack thread has jump links to host logs).

Notes to self (informal):
- When we add long-session synthetic load, try to emulate the exact clients who cause long contexts (tenant prefix sampling).
- Consider setting an explicit per-tenant max-kv-bytes to avoid single-tenant blowups.

Next steps for this doc:
- Convert to final postmortem after root-cause confirmation and when PR revert/patches land.
- Link with product & solutions eng to evaluate customer impact and outreach plan (if needed).

Signed: Aisha Patel (on-call SRE)
